record.paper_title: Selected results and open problems in a semiclassical theory of dense matter
record.original_question: Under static compression, metallic hydrogen had been predicted by the SK theory to appear near 300 GPa, but experiments up to 342 GPa had not shown metallization at the time of this paper, and disorder was suggested as one possible explanation for the mismatch. At what pressure and under what physical conditions, if any, does hydrogen actually undergo metallization under high pressure, and why had the experimentally accessible static-compression regime up to 342 GPa not yet exhibited the metallization expected from theory?

evidence.quote: Static experiments performed at values of pressure P ≤ 342 GPa have not shown signs of metallization of hydrogen [12],so the problem seems (at present)to be completely open.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider solid molecular hydrogen subjected to static high pressure at low temperature. Semiclassical electronic-structure theory predicts a transition to a metallic state at a pressure near 300 GPa, yet diamond-anvil-cell experiments performed at static pressures up to 342 GPa have not observed metallization. Determine the actual pressure (and accompanying thermodynamic conditions—temperature, crystalline vs. fluid phase, ordered vs. disordered configuration) at which hydrogen undergoes a transition to a metallic state under static compression, and provide a physical explanation for why metallization has not been observed in the experimentally accessible static-compression regime up to 342 GPa. In particular, assess whether structural disorder, molecular dissociation barriers, or other mechanisms account for the discrepancy between the theoretical prediction and experiment.
artifact.status_search_result: Dynamic (shock) compression experiments have demonstrated metallization of fluid hydrogen, and some diamond-anvil-cell studies have reported signatures of metallic behavior at very high static pressures (around 400–500 GPa), but a fully reproduced, room-temperature solid metallic hydrogen phase under static compression remains contested. Recent reviews (2024) describe ongoing challenges, with theory now placing solid-phase metallization above ~500 GPa, beyond the 342 GPa range cited as not yet showing metallization. The question is thus partially resolved: metallization is observed in dynamic/fluid regimes, while solid static metallization at room temperature is still an active experimental problem.

status_evidence.title: Metallization of Hydrogen Under High Pressure: Challenges and Experimental Progress (2024)
status_evidence.snippet: Review of challenges and experimental progress in achieving metallic hydrogen under high pressure.
status_evidence.claim: Static metallization of solid hydrogen remains an active and only partially resolved experimental problem as of 2024.

status_evidence.title: Metallic hydrogen - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Solid H2 is not predicted to metallize until static pressure exceeds ~500 GPa; dynamic compression has produced metallic fluid hydrogen.
status_evidence.claim: Theoretical metallization pressure for solid H2 is now estimated above ~500 GPa, beyond the 342 GPa range of earlier static experiments.

status_evidence.title: Dynamic high pressure: Why it makes metallic fluid hydrogen (Nellis)
status_evidence.snippet: Metallic fluid hydrogen achieved by multiple-shock compression at ~140 GPa and 3000 K.
status_evidence.claim: Metallization is achieved in the fluid phase via dynamic compression, distinct from the static solid-phase problem.
